content: A methyl group is a hydrophobic alkyl functional group derived from methane (CH₄). It has the chemical formula -CH₃ and is often abbreviated as -Me in molecular structures. This hydrocarbon unit is commonly found in numerous organic compounds. When positioned to the left of a bond, it is typically written as H₃C; for instance, ethane is represented as H₃C-CH₃. Methyl groups can be introduced into organic compounds through an SN2 reaction involving iodomethane or via the reaction of methyl lithium or methylmagnesium chloride (MeMgCl) with a carbon atom that has a leaving group. The addition of methyl groups to a compound generally increases its lipophilicity while reducing its water solubility. This modification can enhance the compound's ability to be absorbed into biological membranes but may hinder its release from these membranes into aqueous environments. The incorporation of a methyl group can influence the metabolic rate of an analogue in one of three ways: (1) an increased rate of metabolism due to oxidation of the methyl group, (2) an increased rate of metabolism due to demethylation, where the methyl group is transferred to another compound, or (3) a reduction in the metabolic rate of the analogue. The chemical reactivity of a methyl group depends on the nature of the molecule to which it is attached. For example, when part of an alkane, the methyl group is highly unreactive and resists interaction with all but the strongest acids, bases, oxidizing agents, and reducing agents. However, electrophilic reagents can attack the methyl group under certain conditions. For instance, oxidation with permanganate can convert the methyl group into a carboxyl group (-COOH), resulting in the formation of benzoic acid. The methyl radical, CH₃, is a species with an unpaired electron. Although it readily dimerizes to form ethane, it is sufficiently stable (unlike atomic hydrogen) to be observed as a dilute gas. Methyl radicals can be generated through the thermal decomposition of specific compounds, particularly those containing an -N=Nlinkage, which release the highly stable dinitrogen molecule (N₂) upon heating.
